text: Keawe did not believe the story. <break time="0.8s" /> At first. <break time="0.8s" /> So he spoke to the bottle and said. <break time="0.8s" /> I want my fifty dollars back. <break time="0.8s" /> At once his pocket felt heavy again. <break time="0.8s" /> And when he counted the money. <break time="0.8s" /> He found exactly fifty dollars there. <break time="0.8s" /> Next he sold the bottle to a shop. <break time="0.8s" /> For sixty dollars. <break time="0.8s" /> But it did come back. <break time="0.8s" /> For that night. <break time="0.8s" /> It lay in his sea chest. <break time="0.8s" /> Keawe told everything. <break time="0.8s" /> To his friend Lopaka, a fellow sailor. <break time="0.8s" /> Who advised him. <break time="0.8s" /> To go home and wish for something good. <break time="0.8s" /> Back in Hawaii. <break time="0.8s" /> Keawe heard sad news. <break time="0.8s" /> For his uncle had died. <break time="0.8s" /> And his uncles son had drowned at sea. <break time="0.8s" /> Their land and money. <break time="0.8s" /> Now belonged to Keawe. <break time="0.8s" /> And it was exactly the amount. <break time="0.8s" /> That his dream house would cost. <break time="0.8s" /> Soon a grand house. <break time="0.8s" /> With three floors. <break time="0.8s" /> Stood on the mountainside. <break time="0.8s" /> And people called it the Bright House. <break time="0.8s" /> Lopaka wanted to buy the bottle. <break time="0.8s" /> But first he asked to see the imp. <break time="0.8s" /> And when it came out. <break time="0.8s" /> Both men froze with fear. <break time="0.8s" /> Even so. <break time="0.8s" /> Lopaka bought it. <break time="0.8s" /> Because he dreamed of having a ship of his own. <break time="0.8s" /> And he left that very night. <break time="0.8s" /> Keawe slept well. <break time="0.8s" /> For the first time in days. <break time="0.8s" /> Glad that the bottle was no longer his.
